newsitem.title: INDIA: Populous Indian state begins key polls peacefully.
newsitem.headline: Populous Indian state begins key polls peacefully.

text.p: India's northern Uttar Pradesh state began local polls on Monday which analysts said could test Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ability to ride out a challenge from right-wing Hindu nationalists.
Tens of thousands of paramilitary troops were deployed to guard polling booths in the violence-prone state of 140 million people, which borders Tibet and Nepal.

"Polling has started on schedule in each of the 135 constituencies in 21 districts of the state and everything is peaceful," Mohinder Singh, a senior state official, told Reuters. Voting began at 7 a.m. (0130 GMT).
Polling in the remaining constituencies for the 425-member state assembly will be held on October 3 and 7.
Police imposed an around-the-clock curfew in the Moslem-majority quarter of Lucknow, the state capital and the main base of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Four policemen and one woman were injured on Sunday when youths and police clashed in Lucknow, officials said.
Police pulled the body of an unidentified man from a gutter on Saturday after Hindu and Moslem groups clashed last week over the erection of a Hindu idol in Lucknow, the officials said.
Scores of people were injured in the clashes. It was unclear if the man was killed in those clashes.

Politicians said the polls, involving about 100 million eligible voters, would test Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition against the BJP, India's main opposition group which is campaigning for mid-term parliamentary polls.
"It is inevitable now that mid-term polls for parliament will be held sooner than later," BJP President Lal Krishna Advani told reporters in Lucknow on Sunday.

The BJP derives significant strength from Uttar Pradesh where its campaign to build a Hindu temple at the site of a 16th century mosque gave it broad support in several north Indian states and made it the main opposition in parliament in 1991.

Militant supporters of the BJP demolished the Babri mosque in Ayodhya, 200 km (120 miles) east of Lucknow, in December 1992, triggering nationwide Hindu-Moslem riots in which more than 3,000 people died.
Hindu militants say a mosque in the western Uttar Pradesh city of Mathura and another in Varanasi on the state's eastern flank stand on sites of ancient Hindu temples.
While the BJP is playing down the issue in its campaign, the government, taking no chances, has staggered the polls over three days to cover the three disputed sites on different days.
During the assembly polls, Deve Gowda's fractious United Front alliance takes on the Congress, which supports his minority government in Delhi, and the BJP in a triangular fight.
Uttar Pradesh, which is more populous than Japan or Pakistan, sends 85 deputies to the 545-member federal parliament, where the BJP is the biggest single party.
Analysts say the state, once a bastion of the Congress party which has ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947, could help a recent trend of coalition politics.
"We have supported the United Front in Delhi," Congress state spokesman Ramesh Dixit told Reuters on Monday. "It is their turn now to support our government in Uttar Pradesh."
